text: I would now give the floor to his
excellency Mark Harmon nanadu Araba,
chair of delegation of Benon,
President President of the General
Assembly,
Secretary General of the United Nations.
Excellencies, heads of delegation,
ladies and gentlemen,
it is a great honor for me to be
speaking before this august assembly. I
would like to convey to you the warmest
greetings of the Benanese people and to
carry before you the voice of these
people. A voice resolutely committed to
peace, dialogue and multilateralism.
A voice which yearns to fully partake in
our collective reflection about the
future of our organization and the
future of our world.
If I may, at the outset, I would like to
pay a glowing tribute to his excellency
Antonio Guterish.
This is his last general assembly as
Secretary General of the United Nations.
At a time when the temptation to
withdraw to tend inwards is strong. When
many are saying that in the face of
crisis we must do so. No nation can
build lasting security and prosperity
through isolation. I would like to
extend to Mr. Guterish our heartfelt
gratitude.
Thank you for your commitment to serving
humanity. I also wish to extend our
heartfelt congratulations to his
excellency Khalil Rakman, president of
this 81st session. We wish you every
success as you discharge your duties.
Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen,
there are moments in history where we
are compelled to choose not just what we
want to do but also what we want to
become.
It is with this reflection in mind that
Benin is taking part in this session
driven by a deep-seated conviction.
You can't just wait for the future. You
have to prepare for it. Now this
conviction serves as a guide for Benin.
It's also inspired
Benin vision 2060 which is propelling
our nation towards the centenery of uh
our independence. But uh this ambition
does not apply only to the fate of our
nation.
It will also determine the way in which
we view the world. The world which today
stands at a crossroads. We are seeing
wars dragging on. Terrorist threats
making inroads. Persistent geopolitical
tensions, worsening inequality,
debt levels which are reducing the room
for maneuver available to many states,
as well as climate upheaval,
which is hitting the most vulnerable the
hardest.
At the same time, we're witnessing
technological transformation on a vast
scale. It's accelerating. AI is already
transforming knowledge, work, our
economies, education and information.
Never has humanity has never has
humanity had so many different means to
shape its fate. However,
nor has humanity ever been so acutely
aware of the need to make collective
decisions about how these means should
be used to serve the common good. This
is why the theme of this 81st session,
restoring trust, managing
transformation, a UN that delivers for
all
resonates so strongly.
The true challenge of our time is not
just managing a succession of crisis,
but it is restoring our collective
capacity to anticipate to make decisions
to act before these crises become
irreversible.
Mr. President, Benin believes in
multilateralism.
We believe not because we harbor
nostalgia for the world of 1945, but
because in 2026, the world more than
ever needs a forum where states can talk
to one another, listen to one another,
and act in concert. Defending
multilateralism also means taking a le a
lucid look at the United Nations
organization.
Trust indeed is not something you can
order. It takes shape when our
organization can respond to the
expectations of our people, the people
it serves, when the organization can
deliver concrete results. It is in this
spirit that Benin supports the efforts
undertaken within the framework of the
UN80 initiative. We need to achieve
greater efficiency, coherence,
transparency, and responsibility.
Nonetheless, we should remain cognizant
of a key requirement.
Reforming the UN doesn't simply mean
cutting costs. What it should mean is
boosting the organization's impact.
A more effective United Nations should
be better positioned to prevent
conflicts to respond to humanitarian
crisis
to shore up development and anticipate
the transformations which are already
shaping our future. It should also
remain true to the principles which
underpin its legitimacy, universality,
the sovereign equality of states,
solidarity and respect for the UN
charter. Excellencies, ladies and
gentlemen,
there is one reform without which all
the others will remain incomplete.
The reform of the stewardship of
international peace and security. The
security council for the most part
reflects a balance of forces.
The balance of forces in a world which
is no longer today's world. Africa does
not have a permanent seat. This
situation raises raises issues of
justice, equity, and the legitimacy. It
calls into question the very legitimacy
of the entire multilateral system. Benin
would like to reaffirm its unswerving
support for the common African position
set forth in the Zulwini consensus and
the set declaration. We're not demanding
a privilege. We're demanding
for the stewardship of international
peace and security for that stewardship
to be in keeping with the world we claim
to serve. Mr. President for Benin. The
issue of security has a very concrete a
very tangible dimension. Terrorism has
hit our sub region. It seeks to exploit
our vulnerability to take advantage of
our borders and to progressively extend
its clutches to new areas.
Benin understands full well just how
grave this threat is. On this note, I'd
like to solemnly commend the bravery and
commitment of our defense and security
forces as well as the resilience of the
people of Benin. Our response is
resolute. We are strengthening our
defense and security capabilities. We
are bolstering the surveillance of our
territory and our borders. We are also
stepping up our cooperation with our
neighbors and our partners. However, our
region's experience has taught us one
very important lesson.
When faced with the fast evolving
threat, we must act very quickly before
that threat becomes a crisis. For that
reason,
prevention, early warning and upstream
action should all be part and parcel of
our security policy. This requires
better intelligence sharing,
strengthening crossborder cooperation,
improving coordination between national,
subregional and continentwide
mechanisms,
interstate solidarity, regional
cooperation,
the action of the African Union, the
support of the United Nations. We need
all of the above to be better
coordinated.
Education, employment, infrastructure,
and the opportunities offered up to our
young people are also part and parcel of
our efforts aimed at uh preventing the
vulnerabilities, the very
vulnerabilities which terrorist groups
seek to exploit. Excellencies, ladies
and gentlemen, collective security can
only last if we also have economic and
financial security. There is indeed
another source of fragility at the
international level and that is the
fragility of development financing. Many
developing countries are facing a
particularly difficult equation.
They must accelerate their development
and at the same time fund their energy
transition as well as adapt to climate
change on top of investing in health,
education, the digital sphere and
meeting growing social needs.
However, these requirements are piling
up against the backdrop of uh a context
where access to funding is increasingly
costly, where fiscal space is shrinking.
Such a situation is no more sustainable
than it is equitable. Therefore, Benin
calls for ongoing transformation of the
international financial architecture.
The objective being to allow developing
countries to access more accessible,
predictable
financing, financing that is better
tailored to their development
trajectories.
We must also harbor the ambition of
investing more in development because
investing in development is tantamount
to investing in peace, security, and
stability. Mr. President,
the climate issue is an excellent
illustration of this demand for justice.
Africa contributes relatively little to
global greenhouse gas emissions and yet
we are already bearing the full brunt of
climate change.
We're not asking for the right to
pollute. We're asking for the right to
development.
We would like for adaptation,
building resilience and the issue of
loss and damage for all of these to be
addressed urgently given the urgency of
the reality our people are already
facing. We also want for the energy
transition to be an opportunity to
industrialize, to create jobs and
bolster access to energy.
The way we see it, climate justice is
not about pitting development and
transition against one another. It's
about allowing developing countries to
build a growth model that's more
resilient, inclusive, and sustainable.
Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen,
we must also prepare for the next great
transformation,
that of artificial intelligence, AI,
which could become one of the greatest
accelerators of human development. AI
can broaden access to knowledge, improve
health systems, support agricultural
workers, and make state administrations
more efficient. Having said that, AI can
also amplify or exacerbate existing
divides.
If Africa was to solely consume
technologies designed and controlled
outside the continent, a new form of
dependence could emerge linked to data,
infrastructure, computing power, and
critical technologies. We must avoid
this scenario. Therefore, Benin is in
favor of international AI governance
that's inclusive, responsible, and
development oriented.
FA Africa should not just be a market
for
frontier technologies. It should also be
a platform for design, innovation, and
production.
This is the prerequisite for AI to
become not a new driver of divisions but
a tool for achieving emancipation
progress and shared development.
Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen,
trust in international institutions is
also linked to the trust people bestow
upon their own institutions.
For its part, Benin is continuing the
process of consolidating our
institutions in our democratic framework
with full respect for our constitution
and our legal order. We deem stability,
public responsibility, and citizen
participation.
We deem them essential preconditions for
sustainable development. Our experience
confirms our conviction. Robust
institutions
are one of the pillars of peace
infrastructure. We stand convinced that
while we might have different national
trajectories, these trajectories should
nevertheless converge towards the same
end goal, giving all people the
necessary conditions for them to be able
to forge their future living in peace,
dignity, and stability.
Mr. President,
if I may, I would now like to address a
dimension that lies at the very heart of
Benin's identity. Benin is a land of
memory, forged from greatness and
resistance. But we also have a very
tragic, painful history, that of
daughters and sons torn away from their
land, separated from their families, and
sent to different parts of the world,
scattered.
This history has left very deep wounds.
It also
through generations
created a diaspora
whose link with the continent has never
been extinguished. We cannot rewrite
this history nor can we erase the wounds
of the past. But we can decide what we
do with that past and Benin has chosen
to build a bridge. We want to give all
those who wish to do so the opportunity
to rekindle their ties with African
history an opportunity to rebuild a
thriving bond with the continent with
the land of their ancestors from which
they were uprooted.
The possibility
under conditions enshrined in our
legislation to acquire the nationality
of Benin. That is what we're offering.
And this is a dimension that goes beyond
a simple administrative procedure. It is
part and parcel of a desire to rebuild a
relationship to rekindle ties and to
transform a very painful memory into a
forward-looking relationship
to this diaspora living all over the
world looking to Africa. To this
diaspora, Benin would like to say the
following.
You inherited a very painful history,
but you can become the agents of a new
page in our history in which memory will
not just be the memory of something
we've lost, but the starting point from
which you can build something new. It is
with this in mind that Benin in intends
to reconnect with peoples of African
descent. This will not be a simple
return to the past but a step towards a
shared future. Benin doesn't just want
to be a land of memory. We want to be a
land of reunions of transmission to
future generations. A land of the
future. Mr. President, excellencies,
ladies and gentlemen, we're often
tempted to look to the future with
disqu. Let's look to the future with
clarity, confidence, and above all
responsibility. We already know a great
deal about what the future has in store.
The climate will continue to change.
Technologies will continue to transform
our societies and our economies. Africa
will have greater weight in global
demographic and economic equilibria.
Security threats will continue to try
and cross borders.
But we know one thing more than
anything. No state will be able to
tackle these challenges on its own.
So let's prepare. Let's prepare our
countries. Let's prepare our
institutions. Let's get multilateralism
ready.
Above all, let's prepare ourselves
to pass the baton because the
responsibility of a generation is not
just to receive the world
bequath to them from those who came
before. It is also to have the courage,
the vision, the determination to hand
down a better world to those who come
after you. This is the responsibility
that Benin intends to shoulder for us,
for Africa and the United Nations. Let's
restore trust, rebuild our capacity for
working together. Let's manage these
transformations. And that means deciding
to prepare for them rather than simply
enduring them. Let's ensure that the
United Nations serves us all. Which
means that multilateralism once again
becomes a source of strength that it is
of use for the people of the world. This
is the basis for multilateralism's
legitimacy and Benin intends to
contribute to this effort. I thank you.
I thank the chair of delegation of bin.
We have heard the last speaker in the
general debate.
